extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from a legal treatise on (1) when costs and specific expense items are taxable in patent litigation and (2) the scope and limits of equity jurisdiction (injunctions, accounts, and when law is adequate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs for abandoned claims and timing of disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs will not be allowed where claims are abandoned at the trial unless a disclaimer was filed before suit; unreasonable delay in disclaiming may defeat recovery on valid claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If invalid claims co-exist with valid claims and the invalid claims are not disclaimed, valid claims may nevertheless be recovered without costs; but an unreasonable delay in filing a disclaimer can defeat even the valid claims (cases cited: Proctor v. Brill; McCormick v. Seymour; Hall v. Wiles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs when patent expired and disclaimer cannot be filed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where plaintiff recovers on a valid claim but invalid claims were not disclaimed and the patent has expired so that no disclaimer can now be filed, the plaintiff may obtain a decree without costs provided there was no unreasonable delay in disclaiming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On appeal in such situations each party pays their own costs and one half the expense of printing the records (see Tale Lock Co. v. Saigent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of costs among multiple claims or patents
rubrics_metrics.description: When litigation involves multiple claims or multiple patents, costs are apportioned according to who prevails on each claim/patent: if plaintiff recovers on one claim and defendant on another, costs may be apportioned; if only one of two claims is sustained, plaintiff recovers no costs under the statutory provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: where plaintiff recovers on one patent and defendant on another, costs will be apportioned (Pennsylvania Diamond Drill Co. v. Simpson). Where suit is based on several patents and plaintiff recovers on only one, he can have no costs (Schmid v. Sooville Mfg. Co.; American Wood Paper Co. v. Heff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs when defendant was misled about non-infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: No costs will be taxed against a defendant who has been misled by the plaintiff into believing that he did not infringe the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant has been misled into buying the patent by the plaintiff, the defendant cannot recover costs if the patent is defeated (cases: Sarven v. Hall; Bunker v. Stevens). The successful party generally recovers costs unless his conduct renders their allowance unlawful or unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxability of copies of patents and assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of the plaintiff's patent procured by the defendant are not taxable as costs in the defendant's favor because the plaintiff is bound to produce his patent; but copies of assignments of the patent procured by the defendant are taxable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Hathaway v. Roach; Woodruff v. Barney for principles distinguishing types of copies that may or may not be taxed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxability of models, Patent Office copies, and other reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of models in the Patent Office are taxable; models like the plaintiff's device may be included in costs taxation, but other models, machines, or photographs are not taxable; the expense of obtaining a model of the defendant's infringing machine is not taxable among the plaintiff's costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited: Wooster v. Handy; Hussey v. Bradley; Comely v. Marckwald. Distinguish Patent Office copies (taxable) from other reproductions (generally not taxable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegraphic and necessary out-of-pocket expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary telegraphic expenses may be taxed as costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Hossay v. Bradley for telegraphing expenses being taxable when necessary to the litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on marshal fees and mileage
rubrics_metrics.description: A marshal cannot tax mileage for zig-zag travel to reach a witness and is not entitled to fees for serving certain procedural rules (e.g., rule to plead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marshal cannot invent roundabout travel to inflate mileage (Parker v. Bigler); not entitled to fees for serving a rule to plead (Proctor v. Bigler).

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness expenses and taxable attendance/mileage
rubrics_metrics.description: Traveling fees of voluntary witnesses attending without summons are generally not taxable against the loser; witnesses summoned in several suits may claim attendance and mileage in each; witnesses living over 100 miles or from out of district are usually treated as voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: reasonable expenses of a voluntary witness may be taxed when the evidence is taken under agreement of the parties. See Spaulding v. Tucker; Parker v. Bigler; Woodruff v. Barney. The treatise also notes that a witness has mileage for returning home in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenses of attending court and counsel attendance not taxable
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of attending court, and of counsel attending, is not taxable as costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Hussey v. Bradley for the principle that routine attendance expenses for parties and counsel are not taxed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of arguments, reporting, and printing costs generally not taxable
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of copying papers or reporting arguments for the use of the court, and of printing pleadings, evidence, briefs, and lithographing drawings, is not taxable unless incurred by order of the court or by agreement of the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printing costs are only taxable when ordered by the court or agreed to; see Hussey v. Bradley and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of obtaining evidence and deposition taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses required to obtain needed evidence may be taxed under the statute (act of 1858); however, a deposition cannot be taxed if, instead of using it, the party called and examined the witness in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Spaulding v. Tucker for general taxing of evidence-gathering expenses; Hathaway v. Roach for deposition taxation limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity jurisdiction exists where legal remedy is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: A court of equity has jurisdiction in patent infringement cases when the legal remedy is inadequate; equity can grant injunctions, compel discovery, order accounts of profits, and provide other relief necessary to effect complete justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically equity sometimes required prior suit at law, but chancery came to grant injunctions without a prior action at law when the patentee's right was undisputed. Equity jurisdiction rests on fundamental jurisprudential principles independent of legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness and limits of legal vs equitable remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and equitable remedies are not concurrent or interchangeable in patent litigation; where an adequate remedy at law exists, the patentee must seek relief at law and equity will not interfere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The acts of Congress (including the act of 1819 and later statutes) did not abolish the distinction between law and equity. Courts have held that equitable powers are exercisable only where legal relief is inadequate (cases cited: Boot v. Lake Shore & Michigan Southern R.R. Co.; Spring v. Domestic Sewing Mach. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity retains jurisdiction to afford complete relief once invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever equity obtains cognizance of a cause for any purpose it will retain the case until complete relief has been afforded; equity will adjudicate all matters in the cause to provide full protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine led to chancery handling the entire proceedings in many patent suits; a court of equity, once engaged, can finally determine all issues and is reluctant to send issues to a jury except rarely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests for adequacy of legal remedy (when law suffices)
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate remedy at law exists where the sole relief required is compensation for a past injury and can be obtained without equitable aid—examples include fixed license fees or cases where infringement has ceased and defendant made no gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee's measure of compensation is fixed (e.g., license fee), an action at law is the proper remedy. Equity will not intervene where damages at law are adequate (cases: Livingston v. Jones; Densmore v. Tantie Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When equity is appropriate for accounts and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity has jurisdiction to compel discovery (e.g., number of articles made under a license) and to order accounts of profits where a legal action would be inadequate or less complete; equity may retain jurisdiction after death of an infringer to settle accounts (though injunctions may not issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity is favored where an account of profits is more readily and completely settled in equity than at law (Kilbourn v. Sunderland; Kirk v. Du Bois). Equity can order discovery when licensees refuse reporting (Pope Mfg. Co. v. Owsley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity does not ordinarily provide relief for mere contractual damages or to annul licenses for nonpayment
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity generally will not entertain actions where the plaintiff's remedy is merely damages for breach of contract or where the relief sought is simply recovery of royalties; a court of equity will not annul a license solely because the licensee failed to pay royalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the compensation is determinable under contract, the remedy at law is adequate; equity will not annul licenses for non-payment (Crandall v. Piano Mfg. Co.; Consolidated Middlings Purifier Co. v. Wolf).

rubrics_metrics.name: No universal test for equitable necessity—depends on circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no precise and universal test for determining the necessity of equitable interference; the decision depends on the circumstances of the individual case, though certain classes of cases fall clearly on one side or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will not be withheld where justice to the parties requires its application; courts look to final relief needed, the ability of law to provide that relief, and ancillary circumstances (cited authorities and illustrative cases throughout the chapter).
